concepts.name: Thermal radiation
concepts.statement: All normal matter at temperatures above absolute zero emits electromagnetic radiation, a conversion of the body's internal thermal energy into electromagnetic energy, and this emission is called thermal radiation.

concepts.name: Blackbody
concepts.statement: An object that absorbs all radiation falling on it, at all wavelengths, is a blackbody; at a uniform temperature its emission, blackbody radiation, has a characteristic frequency distribution that depends only on the temperature.

concepts.name: Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation
concepts.statement: A body emits radiation at a given temperature and frequency exactly as well as it absorbs the same radiation; otherwise a body in a room at one temperature would grow hotter while the room grew colder, contradicting the second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
concepts.statement: The total power radiated from one square meter of black surface, integrated over all emitted frequencies, goes as the fourth power of the absolute temperature.

concepts.name: Wien's displacement law
concepts.statement: The frequency at which a blackbody's emission is most intense is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, so the peak wavelength is inversely proportional to it.

concepts.name: Spectral energy density
concepts.statement: The energy density of blackbody radiation per unit frequency, so that ρ(ν,T)dν is the energy per unit volume carried by frequencies between ν and ν + dν.

concepts.name: Rayleigh-Jeans law
concepts.statement: Classical physics, treating the radiation in a cavity as oscillators each with energy k_BT, predicts a spectral energy density that grows as the square of the frequency; it agrees with experiment at low frequencies only.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet catastrophe
concepts.statement: Integrated over all frequencies, the Rayleigh-Jeans law predicts that a blackbody radiates infinite energy, an absurd prediction caused by the classical law failing at high frequencies and short wavelengths.

concepts.name: Quantization of energy
concepts.statement: Energy is quantized when a system can hold only certain discrete amounts of it, like a ball on the steps of a ladder, rather than any amount, like a ball on a ramp.

concepts.name: Planck's quantum hypothesis
concepts.statement: Planck assumed that the oscillating electrons in the walls of a blackbody can have only energies that are whole-number multiples of a quantum hν, so energy is absorbed and emitted in these discrete amounts.

concepts.name: Planck's constant
concepts.statement: The constant of proportionality h between the energy of a quantum and its frequency, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

concepts.name: Planck's distribution law
concepts.statement: With the quantum hypothesis, the spectral energy density of blackbody radiation is 8πhν³/c³ times 1/(e^{hν/k_BT} − 1), which agrees with experiment at all frequencies and reduces to the Rayleigh-Jeans law at low frequencies.

concepts.name: Photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: Light shining on a metal surface can eject electrons from it; the energy of the ejected electrons depends on the frequency of the light and not on its intensity, which classical wave theory cannot explain.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.statement: A quantum of electromagnetic radiation, a packet of light carrying the energy hν.

concepts.name: Stopping voltage
concepts.statement: The minimum retarding voltage on the collector plate that stops every ejected photoelectron from getting through, a measure of the electrons' greatest kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Work function
concepts.statement: The minimum energy required to extract an electron from the surface of a metal, characteristic of the metal.

concepts.name: Threshold frequency
concepts.statement: The lowest frequency of light that can eject a photoelectron from a given metal, at which the photon energy just equals the work function.

concepts.name: Einstein's photoelectric equation
concepts.statement: A photon gives all its energy hν to one electron, which spends the work function Φ to leave the metal and keeps the rest as kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Line spectrum
concepts.statement: A spectrum of discrete wavelengths: an excited gas emits light only at the wavelengths characteristic of its atoms, and a cool gas in front of a continuous source absorbs light at the same wavelengths.

concepts.name: Wavenumber
concepts.statement: The reciprocal of the wavelength, the number of waves per unit length, used as a unit of frequency in spectroscopy and usually given in cm⁻¹.

concepts.name: Balmer formula
concepts.statement: Balmer found that the wavelengths of the visible lines of hydrogen fit λ = b n₂²/(n₂² − 4) for integers n₂ greater than 2.

concepts.name: Rydberg formula
concepts.statement: The wavenumbers of every line of the hydrogen spectrum are R_H(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), where n₁ and n₂ are integers with n₂ greater than n₁ and R_H is the Rydberg constant.

concepts.name: Rydberg constant
concepts.statement: The empirical constant R_H of the Rydberg formula, 109,737 cm⁻¹.

concepts.name: Spectral series of hydrogen
concepts.statement: The lines of hydrogen fall into series, each sharing one lower value n₁: the Lyman series in the ultraviolet (n₁ = 1), the Balmer series in the visible (n₁ = 2), and the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series in the infrared.

concepts.name: de Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: De Broglie proposed that any particle of momentum p has a wavelength λ = h/p, as a photon does.

concepts.name: Wave-particle duality
concepts.statement: Light and matter both show the properties of particles and of waves, depending on the experiment.

concepts.name: Interference and diffraction
concepts.statement: Waves passing through two slits or scattered from a regular array interfere, producing bright and dark bands that particles of classical physics would not produce.

concepts.name: Diffraction of matter waves
concepts.statement: Electrons and neutrons scattered from crystals produce diffraction patterns with spacings fixed by their de Broglie wavelengths, the experimental proof of matter waves.

concepts.name: Coulomb potential
concepts.statement: The potential energy of two charges a distance r apart is kQ₁Q₂/r, repulsive when the charges have the same sign and attractive when they have opposite signs, and the force is minus its derivative.

concepts.name: Instability of the planetary atom
concepts.statement: A classical electron orbiting a nucleus is accelerating and must radiate energy, so it would spiral into the nucleus; Rutherford's planetary atom cannot be stable.

concepts.name: Bohr's quantization of angular momentum
concepts.statement: Bohr postulated that the electron's angular momentum in its orbit is restricted to whole-number multiples of ħ.

concepts.name: Bohr model
concepts.statement: The electron in a hydrogen-like atom moves on circular orbits whose angular momentum is quantized, does not radiate while in an orbit, and emits or absorbs a photon only when it jumps between orbits.

concepts.name: Bohr radius
concepts.statement: The radius a₀ = 4πε₀ħ²/(e²m_e) = 52.9 pm of the smallest orbit of the hydrogen atom in the Bohr model.

concepts.name: Bohr energy levels
concepts.statement: In the Bohr model the energy of the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like atom is −Z²/n² times 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, one Rydberg.

concepts.name: Rydberg formula from the Bohr model
concepts.statement: The frequency of the photon emitted when the electron drops from orbit nᵢ to orbit n_f is the energy difference divided by h, which gives the Rydberg formula with its constant in terms of e, m_e, ε₀ and h.

concepts.name: Standing-wave picture of Bohr orbits
concepts.statement: An orbit is allowed when a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths fits around its circumference, so the electron's wave closes on itself; this reproduces Bohr's quantization of angular momentum.

concepts.name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: The position and the momentum of a particle cannot both be known exactly: the product of their uncertainties is at least ħ/2.

concepts.name: Wave packet
concepts.statement: A wave localized in space, built by adding waves of many wavelengths; the narrower the packet, the wider the spread of wavelengths and so of momenta it needs.

concepts.name: Probability in quantum mechanics
concepts.statement: Where a single quantum particle will be detected cannot be predicted exactly; only the probability of detection at each place, which builds up as a pattern over many particles.

concepts.name: Sine wave
concepts.statement: The simplest wave is the one-dimensional sine wave, whose amplitude at position x and time t is A(x,t) = A_o sin(kx − ωt + φ).

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: The maximum amplitude of a wave is the largest distance of the medium from its equilibrium position during one wave cycle, from the crest to the baseline.

concepts.name: Wavenumber (angular)
concepts.statement: The wavenumber k of a sine wave sets how fast its phase advances along x, 2π radians per wavelength.

concepts.name: Angular frequency
concepts.statement: The angular frequency ω of a wave sets how fast its phase advances in time at a fixed position, 2π radians per period.

concepts.name: Phase constant
concepts.statement: The phase constant φ fixes where in its cycle the wave is at x = 0 and t = 0.

concepts.name: Traveling wave
concepts.statement: A traveling wave moves through space and time, carrying energy from one place to another; on a rope it travels at constant speed and keeps its shape, so its displacement is y(x,t) = f(x − vt).

concepts.name: Wave velocity
concepts.statement: The velocity of a wave is the speed at which its shape moves along the medium, the v by which f(x) is shifted to f(x − vt).

concepts.name: Standing wave
concepts.statement: A standing (stationary) wave stays in one place, with crests and troughs at fixed intervals separated by nodes; it only vibrates up and down, and no energy travels along it.

concepts.name: Node
concepts.statement: A node is a point (or line) of a standing wave that does not move while the rest of the medium vibrates.

concepts.name: Antinode
concepts.statement: An antinode is a place of maximum oscillation in a standing wave, halfway between neighbouring nodes.

concepts.name: Classical wave equation
concepts.statement: The displacement u(x,t) of a one-dimensional wave, traveling or standing, obeys the linear partial differential equation ∂²u/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²u/∂t².

concepts.name: Boundary conditions
concepts.statement: Boundary conditions fix what happens at the ends of the medium; for a string of length L held taut at both ends, u(0,t) = 0 and u(L,t) = 0 for all t.

concepts.name: Initial conditions
concepts.statement: Initial conditions fix how the wave is produced: the values of the solution (and its rate of change) at a starting time.

concepts.name: Partial differential equation
concepts.statement: A partial differential equation (PDE) involves a function of two or more independent variables and its partial derivatives; the wave equation is a second-order PDE in x and t.

concepts.name: Ordinary differential equation
concepts.statement: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) contains a function or functions of one independent variable and its derivatives.

concepts.name: Separating the variables of a PDE
concepts.statement: Assume the solution is a product of functions of one variable each, u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), substitute it into the PDE and collect each variable on its own side, turning the PDE into ordinary differential equations; sums of such solutions are solutions of a linear equation.

concepts.name: Separated wave equation
concepts.statement: Substituting u = X(x)T(t) into the wave equation and dividing by XT leaves a side in x only and a side in t only, so each equals one constant K, giving two ordinary differential equations.

concepts.name: Trivial solution
concepts.statement: The trivial solution u = 0 satisfies the equation and its boundary conditions but describes no wave, so it is ignored.

concepts.name: Exponential solutions of a second-order linear equation
concepts.statement: Trying y = e^{αx} in d²y/dx² − k²y = 0 gives α² − k² = 0, so α = ±k and the general solution is any linear combination y = c₁e^{kx} + c₂e^{−kx}.

concepts.name: Euler's formula
concepts.statement: A complex exponential is a combination of a cosine and a sine: e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ.

concepts.name: Oscillatory solutions
concepts.statement: When the separation constant is negative, K = −p², the spatial equation is d²X/dx² + p²X = 0, whose general solution X = Ae^{ipx} + Be^{−ipx} can be written X = c₁ cos(px) + c₂ sin(px).

concepts.name: Quantization by boundary conditions
concepts.statement: Requiring X(0) = 0 and X(L) = 0 forces c₁ = 0 and sin(pL) = 0, so pL = nπ with n = 1, 2, 3, …: only solutions with specific wavelengths exist.

concepts.name: Spatial solutions of a string fixed at both ends
concepts.statement: The spatial part of the wave equation's solution for a string held at zero at both ends is X(x) = D sin(nπx/L), an infinite set distinguished by n.

concepts.name: Quantum number
concepts.statement: A quantum number is the integer parameter, introduced by the boundary conditions, that distinguishes the allowed solutions of a system from each other.

concepts.name: Temporal solutions of a string fixed at both ends
concepts.statement: With K = −(nπ/L)², the temporal equation is d²T/dt² + ω_n²T = 0 with ω_n = nvπ/L, solved by T(t) = E cos(ω_n t) + F sin(ω_n t); no boundary condition fixes E and F.

concepts.name: Normal mode
concepts.statement: Each solution u_n(x,t) = [G_n cos(ω_n t) + H_n sin(ω_n t)] sin(nπx/L) of the wave equation for a string held at both ends is a normal mode, a standing wave with its own frequency.

forms.latex: u_n(x,t) = \left[ G_n \cos (\omega_n t) + H_n \sin (\omega_n t) \right] \sin \left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L} \right)

concepts.name: Fundamental and overtones
concepts.statement: The normal mode with n = 1 is the fundamental; each subsequent mode is an overtone, or harmonic.

concepts.name: Linear differential equation
concepts.statement: A differential equation is linear when the sum of any two of its solutions, and any af + bg with constants a and b, is also a solution.

concepts.name: Principle of Superposition
concepts.statement: The sum of two or more solutions of the wave equation is also a solution: where waves meet, the displacement at each point is the sum of the displacements of the waves singly, which is interference.

concepts.name: General solution as a superposition of normal modes
concepts.statement: Since the wave equation is linear and homogeneous, its total solution for the string is the sum of all its normal modes, u(x,t) = Σ_n [G_n cos(ω_n t) + H_n sin(ω_n t)] sin(nπx/L).

forms.latex: u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( G_n \cos (\omega_n t) + H_n \sin (\omega_n t) \right) \sin \left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)

concepts.name: Frequencies of the normal modes
concepts.statement: The nth normal mode of a string oscillates at the natural frequency ν_n = ω_n/2π = nv/2L, so the more curved the mode, the faster it oscillates.

concepts.name: Wave equation in two and three dimensions
concepts.statement: The displacement of a wave in two or three dimensions obeys the wave equation with one second derivative per spatial direction, ∇²u = (1/v²) ∂²u/∂t², because the medium curves in every direction at once.

forms.latex: \dfrac{ \partial^2 u(x,y,t)}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{ \partial^2 u(x,y,t)}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{1}{v^2} \dfrac{ \partial^2 u(x,y,t)}{\partial t^2}
\dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} = \dfrac{1}{v^2} \dfrac{ \partial^2 u}{\partial t^2}

concepts.name: Laplacian
concepts.statement: The Laplacian ∇² is the shorthand for the sum of the second partial derivatives in space, ∂²/∂x² + ∂²/∂y² + ∂²/∂z².

concepts.name: Wave vector
concepts.statement: The wave vector k points in the direction a harmonic wave in three dimensions is moving; its magnitude is |k| = √(k_x² + k_y² + k_z²).

concepts.name: Harmonic plane wave
concepts.statement: The three-dimensional wave equation has harmonic solutions u = A sin(k_x x + k_y y + k_z z − ωt) with ω = v|k|, the form of the fields in a radio or light wave.

forms.latex: u(x,y,z,t) = A \sin (k_x x +k_y y +k_z z -\omega t)

concepts.name: Modes of a rectangular membrane
concepts.statement: Separating variables with the edges held fixed gives the modes of a rectangular membrane of length a and width b, u = A_nm cos(ω_nm t + φ_nm) sin(n_xπx/a) sin(n_yπy/b), with one quantum number in each dimension.

concepts.name: Nodal line
concepts.statement: On a two-dimensional membrane the nodes are lines that do not move: straight lines across a rectangle, and diameters (angular nodes, at fixed angles) and circles (radial nodes, at fixed radii) on a circle.

concepts.name: Bessel function
concepts.statement: Bessel functions J_m are oscillatory functions that give the radial shape of the modes of a circular membrane.

concepts.name: Modes of a circular membrane
concepts.statement: The modes of a circular membrane, in polar coordinates, are u(r,θ,t) = J_m(λ_mn r) cos mθ cos cλ_mn t, with two quantum numbers m and n that play the roles of n_x and n_y.

forms.latex: u(r, \theta, t)=J_{m}\left(\lambda_{m n} r\right) \cos m \theta \cos c \lambda_{m n} t

concepts.name: Wavefunction
concepts.statement: The solution of a wave equation, a function of the space coordinates x, y, z and the time t, is called the wavefunction; for a particle it is the amplitude of its matter wave.

concepts.name: Reduced Planck's constant
concepts.statement: Planck's constant divided by 2π, ħ ≡ h/2π, introduced by Dirac because h occurs in most formulas with the denominator 2π.

concepts.name: Free-particle matter wave
concepts.statement: Replacing ν and λ in a traveling wave by E/h and h/p gives the wave of a particle of energy E and momentum p moving in the x direction.

concepts.name: Schrödinger equation for a free particle
concepts.statement: The wavefunction of a free particle, on which no force acts, satisfies iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²Ψ/∂x², which follows from E = p²/2m.

concepts.name: Time-dependent Schrödinger equation
concepts.statement: The wavefunction of a particle of mass m in a potential energy V that depends on position only obeys iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = [−(ħ²/2m)∇² + V]Ψ; the equation is postulated, not derived.

concepts.name: Stationary state
concepts.statement: For a conservative system, whose energy is constant, the wavefunction separates into a space-only factor ψ(r) and a phase factor e^{−iEt/ħ} of constant magnitude.

concepts.name: Time-independent Schrödinger equation
concepts.statement: The space-only wavefunction ψ of a state of energy E satisfies [−(ħ²/2m)∇² + V]ψ = Eψ: the total energy is the kinetic energy plus the potential energy.

concepts.name: Operator
concepts.statement: An operator is a rule for turning one function into another, as a function is a rule for turning one number into another; it is often marked by a hat.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian operator
concepts.statement: The operator of the time-independent Schrödinger equation, Ĥ = −(ħ²/2m)∇² + V, which corresponds to the total energy of the system.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue equation
concepts.statement: An equation in which an operator acting on a function gives a constant times the same function.

concepts.name: Eigenfunction
concepts.statement: A function that solves an eigenvalue equation of an operator; eigen is the German word for self or own.

concepts.name: Eigenvalue
concepts.statement: The constant that multiplies the eigenfunction in an eigenvalue equation.

concepts.name: Operator algebra
concepts.statement: Operators add and multiply by acting on a function in turn: (Â ± B̂)f = Âf ± B̂f, ÂB̂f = Â[B̂f]; the associative law holds, but the commutative law does not in general.

concepts.name: Commutator
concepts.statement: The commutator of Â and B̂ is ÂB̂ − B̂Â; the operators commute when it is zero, and then the order of operating does not matter.

concepts.name: Linear operator
concepts.statement: An operator Ô is linear when Ô(f + g) = Ôf + Ôg and Ô(cf) = cÔf for any constant c, real or complex; most operators of quantum mechanics are linear.

concepts.name: Hermitian operator
concepts.statement: An operator Â is Hermitian, or self-adjoint, when ∫f*Âg dτ = (∫g*Âf dτ)* for all functions f and g that obey the specified boundary conditions.

concepts.name: The Hamiltonian is Hermitian
concepts.statement: Integrating by parts twice, with the boundary terms vanishing, shows that the particle-in-a-box Hamiltonian satisfies the Hermitian condition.

concepts.name: Operators of observables are Hermitian
concepts.statement: It is postulated that all quantum-mechanical operators that represent dynamical variables are Hermitian.

concepts.name: Observables are eigenvalues
concepts.statement: Every experimental measurable a is an eigenvalue of a specific operator Â, Âψ = aψ; the eigenvalues are the possible measured values, often only a subset of what classical mechanics allows.

concepts.name: The Schrödinger equation as an eigenvalue problem
concepts.statement: The time-independent Schrödinger equation Ĥψ = Eψ is an eigenvalue equation of the Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues are the allowed total energies.

concepts.name: Correspondence principle
concepts.statement: Bohr's principle that the behavior of systems described by quantum theory reproduces classical physics in the limit of large quantum numbers; the Hamiltonian follows from p²/2m + V by replacing p with −iħ d/dx.

concepts.name: Linear momentum operator
concepts.statement: The operator of the linear momentum of a particle moving along x, p̂ₓ = −iħ ∂/∂x, and −iħ∇ in three dimensions.

concepts.name: Position operator
concepts.statement: The operator of the position of a particle is multiplication by the coordinate: x̂ = x, and r̂ = r in three dimensions.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy operator
concepts.statement: The quantum counterpart of p²/2m: KÊ = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²/∂x², and −(ħ²/2m)∇² in three dimensions.

concepts.name: Angular momentum operator
concepts.statement: The cross product of the position and momentum operators, L̂ = −iħ(r × ∇).

concepts.name: Eigenstate
concepts.statement: A system whose wavefunction is an eigenfunction of an operator is in an eigenstate of that observable, and a measurement gives the eigenvalue; eigenstate and wavefunction are often used interchangeably.

concepts.name: A wavefunction as a superposition of eigenstates
concepts.statement: A wavefunction that is not an eigenstate of an operator can usually be written as a sum of its eigenstates, ψ = Σ cᵢφᵢ.

concepts.name: Collapse of the wavefunction
concepts.statement: A measurement leaves the wavefunction in an eigenstate of the measured observable, and only eigenvalues are observed: the wavefunction collapses into an eigenstate.

concepts.name: Square of the modulus
concepts.statement: The product of a wavefunction and its complex conjugate, Ψ*Ψ = |Ψ|², which is real.

concepts.name: Probability density
concepts.statement: The probability per unit volume of finding the particle at a point; in one dimension, per unit length.

concepts.name: Born interpretation
concepts.statement: Born proposed in 1926 that the square of the modulus of the wavefunction is the probability density of the particle: the wavefunction is a probability amplitude, and |ψ|² dτ the probability of finding the particle in the volume element dτ.

concepts.name: Volume element
concepts.statement: The element dτ a probability density is integrated over, written in the coordinates adopted: dx dy dz in Cartesian, r² sin φ dr dθ dφ in spherical, r dr dφ dz in cylindrical coordinates.

concepts.name: Probability of finding a particle in a region
concepts.statement: The probability that a measurement finds a particle between a and b is the integral of |ψ|² from a to b, the area under the probability density; in three dimensions the integral runs over the volume.

concepts.name: Well-behaved wavefunction
concepts.statement: A valid wavefunction is single-valued, finite and continuous everywhere; these conditions restrict the solutions of the Schrödinger equation so that only certain energies are allowed.

concepts.name: Particle in a box
concepts.statement: A particle free to move between two impenetrable walls, the simplest non-trivial application of the Schrödinger equation and one that can be solved exactly.

concepts.name: Potential of a one-dimensional box
concepts.statement: The potential energy is zero between x = 0 and x = L and infinite outside, so the particle cannot be found outside the box.

forms.latex: V(x)=\begin{cases} 0 & 0\leq x\leq L \\ \infty & x< 0 \; \text{and}\; x> L \end{cases}

concepts.name: Energy levels of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The boundary conditions ψ(0) = ψ(L) = 0 allow only kL = nπ, so the energy of a particle in a box is quantized, Eₙ = h²n²/8mL² with n = 1, 2, 3, …

concepts.name: Ground state
concepts.statement: The state of lowest energy of a quantum system.

concepts.name: Zero-point energy
concepts.statement: The energy of the ground state in excess of the classical minimum; a particle in a box keeps E₁ = h²/8mL² > 0, and the motion with this energy is the zero-point motion.

concepts.name: Wavefunctions of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The normalized eigenfunctions of a particle in a box are ψₙ(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), the same in form as the standing waves on a string.

concepts.name: Normalization condition
concepts.statement: A wavefunction is normalized when the integral of |ψ|² over all space is 1, since a measurement of the position must find the particle somewhere.

concepts.name: More nodes, higher energy
concepts.statement: The nth state of a particle in a box has n − 1 nodes; more nodes mean sharper curvature and a larger second derivative, so it is generally true that the energy of a quantum state rises with its number of nodes.

concepts.name: Orthogonality
concepts.statement: Two functions are orthogonal when the integral of the product of one's complex conjugate with the other over all space is zero.

concepts.name: Kronecker delta
concepts.statement: δₘₙ is 1 when m = n and 0 when m ≠ n.

concepts.name: Orthonormality
concepts.statement: A set of functions that are each normalized and orthogonal to one another, ∫ψₘψₙ dx = δₘₙ, is orthonormal.

concepts.name: The particle-in-a-box eigenfunctions are orthonormal
concepts.statement: The eigenfunctions of a particle in a box satisfy ∫₀ᴸ ψₘψₙ dx = δₘₙ; orthogonality follows from sin α sin β = ½[cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)].

concepts.name: Normalizing a wavefunction
concepts.statement: Multiplying a wavefunction by the constant that makes the integral of its square modulus over all space equal to 1.

concepts.name: Square-integrable wavefunction
concepts.statement: A wavefunction whose integral of |ψ|² over all space converges, so that it can be normalized; a plane wave is not square-integrable.

concepts.name: Normalization is kept in time
concepts.statement: A square-integrable wavefunction that is normalized at one instant stays normalized as it evolves by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, since the boundary term vanishes as |x| → ∞.

concepts.name: Expectation value
concepts.statement: The probabilistic expected value of a measurement, the weighted average of all possible values, ⟨s⟩ = Σ s(i)Pₛ(i); it need not be a possible value itself.

concepts.name: Quantum expectation value
concepts.statement: The average of an observable o over many measurements on a state ψ is ⟨o⟩ = ∫ψ*Ôψ dx: the probability weights become |ψ|² and the scalar becomes the operator.

concepts.name: Average energy
concepts.statement: The average total energy ⟨H⟩ = ∫ψ*Ĥψ dx is the average kinetic energy plus the average potential energy.

concepts.name: Average position of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The probability density of a particle in a box is symmetric about the center, so ⟨x⟩ = L/2.

concepts.name: Average momentum of a particle in a box
concepts.statement: The average momentum of a particle in a box is zero in every state, though its kinetic energy is not: it is equally likely to move in the +x and −x directions.

concepts.name: Momentum eigenfunctions
concepts.statement: e^{ikx} and e^{−ikx} are eigenfunctions of the momentum operator with eigenvalues +ħk and −ħk, waves moving right and left; the sine of a particle in a box is a combination of the two.

concepts.name: Uncertainty of an observable
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in a quantity A for a wavefunction is ΔA = √(⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩²), from the expectation values of Â² and Â.

concepts.name: Particle in a three-dimensional box
concepts.statement: Separating ψ = X(x)Y(y)Z(z) turns the 3D box into three 1D boxes: ψ is a product of three sines and E = (h²/8m)(nₓ²/Lₓ² + n_y²/L_y² + n_z²/L_z²).

concepts.name: Degeneracy
concepts.statement: An energy level is degenerate when several different stationary states or wavefunctions have its energy, and non-degenerate when only one does.

concepts.name: Degree of degeneracy
concepts.statement: The number of independent wavefunctions for the stationary states of an energy level.

concepts.name: Degeneracy in a cube
concepts.statement: In a cube the energy depends only on nₓ² + n_y² + n_z², so states whose quantum numbers are permutations of one another share an energy: the first excited level is triply degenerate.

concepts.name: Accidental degeneracy
concepts.statement: A degeneracy that arises not from a symmetry such as Lₓ = L_y but from different combinations of nₓ²/Lₓ², n_y²/L_y² and n_z²/L_z² giving the same sum.
